title: Erasmus Mundus Scholarship: The Complete Guide (2027 Intake)
content:
The Erasmus Mundus Joint Master (EMJM) scholarship is the European Union's flagship fully funded master's award: €1,400 per month for 12 to 24 months, tuition fully covered, insurance included, travel supported — and a degree built across two or more European universities in a single programme. This guide covers what the scholarship actually pays in 2026-27, who is eligible, and how to build an application that survives programmes' single-digit acceptance rates.

What the scholarship pays, in real numbers

The student scholarship has two parts. First, participation costs: tuition, library and lab fees are paid to the consortium in full. Second, the student's own package: a monthly allowance of €1,400 for the duration of the master's (12 to 24 months depending on programme), plus travel and installation support where the programme provides it, plus mandatory insurance. Glasgow's Erasmus Mundus page states the arithmetic plainly: €1,400 × 24 months = €33,600 maximum grant per student, on top of covered tuition. Around 100-160 active EMJM programmes run in any cycle, and roughly 2,000-3,000 scholarships are awarded across the portfolio each year — single programmes typically fund 15 to 30 students per intake, which is where the single-digit acceptance rates come from.

[[chart:emjm-package]]

How the programme model works

Every EMJM is a consortium — at least three institutions in at least three countries — delivering one integrated curriculum with mandatory mobility: you study at two, sometimes three, universities and graduate with a joint degree or a double degree. The design is deliberate: the EU funds the cross-border structure, so the scholarship buys you an academic migration story as much as a degree. Practical consequences: you apply to the programme (not to universities separately), you arrange visas for multiple countries, and you build two supervisors' networks in two systems inside two years.

Application rules are strict. You may apply to a maximum of three EMJM programmes in one cycle. At least one of your study periods must differ from your country of residence, and the scholarship cannot fund a second EMJM degree if you already hold one. Some programmes enforce a nationality-balance cap so no single country exceeds roughly 10 per cent of a cohort's scholarships — which, depending on your passport, can work for or against you in a given year.

[[chart:emjm-timeline]]

Eligibility and the calendar

Eligibility basics: a completed (or final-year) bachelor's degree in a relevant field, and any programme-specific requirements — prerequisites, GPAs, language scores set per consortium. The application window for most programmes runs from October to January for a September start, with individual programmes setting their own dates inside that band. Decisions typically land between March and May. Because the scholarship is decided by the consortium's selection committee against its own criteria, the decisive documents are consistent: transcripts, language evidence, two references and a motivation letter scored against the programme's published objectives.

The consortium's side: how selection actually runs

Knowing the machinery helps you aim. Each EMJM consortium forms a selection committee — academic leads from the partner universities plus external experts — that scores applications against criteria published in the call: academic merit, relevance of prior study, motivation fit, references and language evidence, each with its own weight. Two behaviours are universal: eligibility is checked mechanically first (degree, language, the three-programme rule enforced centrally), then candidates are ranked on the motivation letter's specificity and the referees' concrete attestation. Interview stages exist at some programmes and test the same thing the letter should have shown — whether you understand the mobility design you are volunteering for.

Outcomes arrive in tiers: scholarship offers, admission without scholarship (a self-funded place in the same programme — worth checking against your budget, because the degree is identical), and a waitlist that moves between March and May as funded candidates decline. The waitlist is real; holders of a second funded offer who plan to decline should notify the consortium early — a courtesy that moves someone's year forward.

After the offer: the acceptance calculus

An EMJM offer compresses big decisions into short windows, so pre-compute the answers. Programme fit: which specialisation track and which thesis direction would you actually choose — write it down before the offer, because decision deadlines rarely stretch past three weeks. Money: €1,400 a month against the specific cities on your track, plus the savings buffer you hold. Career: the EMJM's distinctive currency is the two-country academic network and the joint-degree credential; for applicants targeting European doctoral positions — MSCA networks pay €4,010 a month and recruit heavily from EMJM cohorts — the master's is a deliberate first step of a longer plan, not a destination. Decide which plan you are on before the clock starts.

An application that clears single-digit odds

Portfolio logic beats perfectionism. Three programme applications — the maximum — spanning one ambitious, one realistic and one broader-field programme give better expected value than three variants of the same dream programme. Inside each application, the motivation letter must name the consortium's actual structure: the mobility track you would follow, the specialisation you would choose at each university, and the thesis direction that connects them. Generic motivation letters are the first filter's easiest discard, because the EMJM model rewards applicants who demonstrably understand the multi-country design they are applying to.

References deserve the four-week treatment (brief, deadline, criteria, what to attest), and language evidence should be settled before October — test seats vanish in peak season. Transcripts and translations are the silent schedule-killers: certified translations of non-English documents take two to six weeks, so order them in September for January deadlines. If the outcome is rejection, the consoling arithmetic is real: a strong EMJM file is the same file that wins DAAD, national and university scholarships, so the work re-enters the market within months rather than dying in one decision.

[[chart:emjm-odds]]

What the money buys in each host city

€1,400 a month reads differently across the consortium map. In typical programme cities — Groningen, Ghent, Aix-en-Provence, Bologna, Tartu — the allowance covers a room, food, transport and insurance with a modest margin, matching how European student budgets actually run. In high-cost nodes that some programmes route through — Paris, Amsterdam, parts of the Nordics — the allowance is tighter and the programme's housing support matters more than the headline rate. The practical check before ranking programme preferences: take each mobility track's cities, price a room on the local market, and confirm the consortium's housing arrangements for scholarship holders. Two programmes with identical allowances can differ by €300 a month in lived costs.

The tuition coverage is worth naming separately because it is invisible money: EMJM participation costs run €9,000-18,000 per year at many consortia, paid directly by the programme. Over 24 months that is €18,000-36,000 you never invoice — on top of the €33,600 allowance cap, the true package value sits near €55,000-70,000, which is why Erasmus Mundus remains Europe's most generous taught-master's funding despite the single-digit odds.

[[chart:emjm-cost-cities]]

Visa and mobility logistics across two countries

The two-country design adds one administrative layer ordinary master's students never meet: sequential visas. Your first residence permit covers the entry country; the consortium issues the documents for the second country's permit mid-programme, and the timing is managed but not magic — keep passport validity beyond the full programme, keep every enrolment certificate, and expect a biometric appointment in your second country. Non-EU students should also ask about the Erasmus+ mobility guarantee arrangements some consortia use to smooth the transition. None of this is difficult; all of it is easier when the first visa is applied for the moment the offer lands rather than the month before term.

Questions applicants often ask

How much is the Erasmus Mundus scholarship per month?

€1,400 per month for the length of the master's (12-24 months), with tuition and participation costs paid in full, insurance included and travel/installation support where provided — a maximum of €33,600 in allowances across 24 months, per Glasgow's published figures.

How many Erasmus Mundus programmes can I apply to?

Three per admission cycle, maximum. Choose them across ambition tiers and tailor each motivation letter to that consortium's mobility track and specialisations — triple-submitting the same letter wastes the cap.

Is the Erasmus Mundus scholarship fully funded?

Yes within its scope: tuition, a monthly living allowance of €1,400, insurance and travel support. It does not pay dependants' costs, and living costs above the allowance — especially in high-rent capitals — come from savings, so read the host cities on your shortlist before accepting an offer.

Official sources and further reading

Programme rules and amounts are set per consortium within the Erasmus+ framework; the programme catalogue and each programme's page are binding. Verify current details before applying.
